title: Across Political Divide, Americans Agree on One Thing: AI Is Moving Too Fast
snippet: Fresh polling shows rare bipartisan consensus as a majority of Americans express deep anxiety over artificial intelligence, job displacement, and local data center development.
content:
In an era defined by hyper-partisanship, the American public has found an unexpected point of unity: deep skepticism and growing alarm over artificial intelligence. From existential fears to concerns over everyday job stability, broad majorities of voters across the political spectrum now agree that AI development is moving at a dangerous pace.

The surge in public anxiety follows a turbulent week for the tech industry after Jacob Coxon, a researcher at AI startup Anthropic, resigned and publicly warned that industry insiders earnestly fear catastrophic risks before the decade concludes. The disclosure triggered renewed calls for federal intervention and sparked intense debate across Capitol Hill.

A Rare Bipartisan Consensus

New survey data reveals that fears surrounding AI are far from fringe. According to a recent Politico poll, 63% of U.S. adults believe there is at least a moderate risk that advanced AI could destroy humanity. That sentiment spans the political aisle, shared by 70% of voters who backed Kamala Harris in 2024 and 60% of those who voted for Donald Trump. Moreover, nearly half of all Americans (48%) support pausing the development of advanced AI models to assess potential threats.

Beyond existential dread, everyday economic anxieties are fueling the backlash. Nearly three-quarters of Americans (73%) say they are concerned about mass unemployment driven by automation. Furthermore, public discomfort extends to practical applications, with strong majorities rejecting the use of AI for medical diagnoses, criminal justice predictions, and administrative government decisions.

Backlash Hits Local Neighborhoods

The pushback is also hitting the physical infrastructure required to power the AI boom. To keep up with massive computing demands, tech firms have accelerated the construction of giant data centers across the country. However, public support for these projects has cratered.

According to polling from Heatmap, 75% of Americans now oppose having a data center built in their local community—a massive jump from a year ago when public opinion was evenly split. Driving the opposition are growing worries over skyrocketing electricity demands, local water consumption, and environmental degradation, leading a majority of Americans to support strict caps on new data center facilities.

Washington Struggle to Match Public Sentiment

Despite the groundswell of public concern, President Donald Trump has rejected calls for tighter guardrails, arguing that aggressive AI expansion is essential for national economic dominance. Yet, voters appear out of sync with the White House's posture. A snap YouGov survey shows that 55% of Americans disapprove of the president's handling of AI, while only 28% approve.

The issue has catalyzed unprecedented political alliances. At a recent "Pro-Human Assembly" in Washington, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and former Trump strategist Steve Bannon both called for immediate federal limits on artificial intelligence before the technology surpasses human control.

With voters on both sides of the aisle demanding urgent guardrails, Capitol Hill faces a rare moment of broad consensus—and mounting pressure to act before public patience runs out.
